WHAT MIGHT A CONTRACT STIPULATE?

FIVE COMPONENTS should be, at least, required for a contract: 1) A substantial (15-20 p.) paper or project (of equivalent time/effort: c. 20 hours) should be defined and outlined. 2) It should be required that the student share the knowledge/skills/experienc- es gained through the paper or project with an audience, either in the class or elsewhere. 3) The contract should include a plan for how the faculty member and student have regular contact outside of class to discuss the student’s progress and an- swer questions regarding the paper or project. 4)The student should be required to state specifically on the contract form how they will meet each of the three NCHC requirements of “broader, deeper, more complex.” 5) A date at the midpoint of the semester should be determined at which the faculty member should provide a brief report to honors administration on the contact they have had with the student and assess the student’s progress to date. (See: Bolsch 2005: 55) CONTRACTS EXEMPLIFY THE BEST OF HONORS PEDAGOGY when, anchored in the tutorial model, they cultivate personalized, mentored learning and ensure consistent, documented quality (Myers and Whitebread, 22).

It is therefore important that honors administrators and advisors keep a close eye on the contracts created, their implementation, and progress, and provide solid templates and rubrics for their creation and use.
While contract courses do not always provide a venue for honors students to interact with each other, they do create space for students to collaborate with instructors and develop important mentoring relationships (Wyatt, 215).
This outcome–a “win-win” if well managed–must be continually emphasized to both faculty and students.
An inclusive pedagogical practice opens the curriculum to a wide array of fac- ulty who become stakeholders in honors.
It has been shown that these curricular practices have led to greater acceptance of and appreciation for honors colleges on campuses where faculty participation is widespread (Wyatt, 196).
Honors administration must therefore constantly work toward an awareness of these practices among all faculty at the University, whether they teach honors students or not.
WHAT ARE EXAMPLES OF POSITIVE OUT- COMES FROM THE USE OF CONTRACTS?

Contracts must be well managed and assessed at the honors admin. level so that they be the effective tool that they are.
Contracts foster and sup- port a sense of community and ownership around hon- ors programs.
The contract should define the contracted project, its deliverables and intended outcomes and deadlines, as well as points of contact and required feedback by the faculty supervisor.
Maintain the awareness that contracts are a venue for meaningful student-faculty relationships. 4

WHAT ARE EXAMPLES OF POSSIBLE PROBLEMS THAT APPEAR WHEN USING CONTRACTS AND WHAT ARE PATHS TOW ARD AVOIDING THEM?
PROBLEMS THAT APPEAR ARE NOT INSURMOUNTABLE.
Mostly they are cir- cumvented by a continuing awareness of processes and a care for good structures and assessment, creating contracts that enhance rather than concede the honors experience (Bambina, 122).
Contracts must not become “routine” or commonplace, no matter what their number.
Nor can they become a “secret fix” only available to those “in the know.” The narrow definition of honors programs can lead to charges of elitism and segre- gation if honors students, who increasingly tend to be upper-middle-class, white, and female, become insulated from the general student population in an honors curricular bubble.
The contract approach mitigates this by allowing students to learn in an in- clusive campus-wide environment while still engaging in an honors curriculum and community (Wyatt, 196).
Overworked instructors may agree to contracts but then require little more than comple- tion of extra assignments with minimal instructor-student interaction.

Honors educators have the responsibility to eliminate underdeveloped honors contracts that dilute rather than enrich the academic experiences of students. (Wyatt, 195.) It is good practice for evaluation and assessment templates to be created and provided by the honors organiza- tion.
And oversight of contracts by honors administrators must therefore be well-struc- tured, mandated, and clear, and guidelines must be provided to faculty on deadlines and assessment rubrics.
It is essential that contracted work not simply be “more”; rather, it must be meaningful- ly integrated in each case with the course content and learning goals and the work the course already requires. (Bahls, 177) The contract must therefore measurably outline work that leads to the “broader, deeper, and more complex learning-centered and learn- er-directed experiences” with which the NCHC defines honors education (NCHC).

The suggestion that the learning experience of a contracted class is equivalent to a stand-alone honors class—seeing as the student receives academic credit for both— opens honors programs and colleges up to potential exploitation by administrators who may not see the need for assigning appropriate resources to honors or may even try to cut budgets. (Badenhausen, 11) It must therefore be agreed—and practiced—that when options are limited, contracts are a workable path to honors completion that benefits both the students and the institution, not a work-around for the program or institution to avoid curriculum development and creating classes.
But even though the close community of students and faculty that defines honors edu- cation is achieved here by other means, the importance of achieving a sense of belong- ing to the larger cohort should not be ignored.
Therefore, a stricture should be in place that students be limited in the number of credits they can complete through contracts, especially in their freshman and sophomore years.

Finally, with increasing demands and tightening budgets overburdening faculty with unpaid work that is not recognized in reviews, it is essential that faculty be recognized and compensated for the additional work a contract entails.
Otherwise, faculty fatigue may set in and departments and colleges may resent the outside burdens (Bambina, 118).
The equivalent of a one-credit independent study would seem reasonable, and perhaps an amendment to faculty contracts might state the value of this work for pro- motion and tenure reviews.
Contracts bring honors students into non-honors classrooms, mitigating the separation of honors stu- dents from others.
Contracts are a beneficial part of the honors methods in individual cases, not a substitute for the program.
Students should be a part of an honors cohort, con- tacts should not be allowed to separate them from the group.
Administration must take care to never let contracts become routine or a “secret fix.” Honors admin. must work diligently to maintain high standards, and clear expec- tations Contract-work must mea- surably achieve NCHC goals: broader, deeper, and more complex learning experiences.
Faculty must be rewarded for the work they do, lest fatigue or resentment under- mine the contract system. 5

NOTES ON DISTINGUISHED HONORS FACULTY FELLOWS DRAFT 01, February 13th 2024 These notes are largely based on—and inspired by—the National Collegiate Honors Council’s “Shared Principles and Practices of Honors Education.” Honors faculty are selected based on their preparation for and commitment to the pedagogy and curriculum of the program or college, their ability to provide intellectual leadership and mentoring for diverse students, and willingness to support the mission of honors.
Selection processes help support the hiring of faculty and professional staff who have been historically underrepresented in higher education, as noted in NCHC’s Diversity and Inclusion Statement. (NCHC Shared Principles and Practices of Honors Education, 5) The Honors Program at URI is designed to support students and faculty in exploring innovative teaching methods.
The interdisciplinary nature of Honors, along with students' self-selection into a challenging and exploratory program, makes it an ideal space for educational innovation.
The program encourages faculty to engage in scholarship on novel educational practices, aligning with the National Collegiate Honors Council's (NCHC) guidelines.

We aim to collaborate with the Office for Advancement of Teaching and Learning (ATL) to assist faculty in developing creative and effective teaching strategies and supporting them in providing intellectual leadership and mentorship to diverse students.
Honors faculty will be chosen based on their commitment to the program's pedagogy and curriculum.
Selected faculty will be asked to participate in–and contribute to–sessions fostering collaboration, sharing ideas, and exploring high-impact practices.
The focus will be on aligning classroom and curriculum-building skills with the goals of URI's Honors Program and the best practices outlined by the NCHC.
The Honors Program, guided by the NCHC, emphasizes student focus, individual development, and leadership skills, prompting faculty discussions on tailoring the student experience to encourage students to take responsibility for their direction and productivity in learning.
This involves, among other things, incorporating hands-on experiences, fostering liberal arts skills, and promoting student success across disciplines.

Recognizing students' diverse backgrounds and learning differences, portions of the workshops will focus on cultural competency and inclusive pedagogies.
In line with NCHC recommendations, Distinguished Faculty Fellows will ensure the representation of historically underserved populations in course materials.
Workshops will investigate inclusive teaching practices in course design, syllabus construction, classroom climate, learning activities, and assessment methods.
Faculty will be encouraged to incorporate diversity, equity, inclusion, and global understanding into their courses, and to engage students in community-based learning and research into local manifestations of global issues.

The Honors Program will be assessed regularly.
Given this, workshops will include a brief introduction to program assessment methods, and help faculty align their courses with the Honors Program’s learning outcomes.
Sessions will also delve into the history and purpose of honors programs, as well as the URI Honors Program's strategic plan and core values.
Faculty will explore incorporating these elements into their courses with a disciplinary focus.
HONORS FACULTY FELLOWS We will initiate a cohort of Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows, excellent instructors who strive to be exemplary student-focused educators.
Selection Process There will be different pathways that lead to the nomination of a teacher to become a Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow.
For example, for specific needs, we will reach out directly to a department for suggestions on who might be qualified and available to teach a needed course.
We will also have general needs for courses that meet our program requirements, at which point we will send out a call for nominations to deans and department chairs.

We will publicly announce the newest Distinguished Faculty Fellows at our annual Distinguished Fellows Dinner to be held every spring.
The nomination process will occur twice a year to coincide with the annual review process – in February for tenure-stream faculty members, and in April for teaching-professor-stream faculty.
Each chosen Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow will serve one three-year term, renewable upon mutual agreement and successful completion of the first term.

Department/College nomination Nominations to become a Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow will be made by department chairs and deans and they should be based on the following criteria: ● teaching excellence awards (not mandatory but certainly preferred) ● high average IDEA evaluations in the category of “Progress on Relevant Objectives” ● strong annual review teaching dossier, including, if possible, classroom observations ● nomination by the department, supported by the dean Interest letter and interview Once a faculty member has been nominated by their department and college dean, we will ask the faculty member: 1) to submit an interest letter and CV; 2) meet the Honors administrative team for an interview; 3) to submit a course proposal that adheres to the following guidelines: ● It meets the 4 Honors program outcomes tied to: creative problem solving, social innovation, interconnection and policy advocacy. ● It echoes the best practices in Honors course design as set forth by the NCHC.. ● It is a course proposal that meets the curricular needs of the Honors program.
Privileges

Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows will: ● Become part of an exclusive cohort of distinguished teaching faculty at URI. ● Teach the best students at the University in small-section courses. ● Bring the revenue generated from HPR or H-section courses back to home department and college ● Participate with other distinguished faculty in Distinguished Honors Teaching Studios held throughout the year. ● Be valued by URI’s Provost through the teaching section of their annual review. ● Receive annual recognition of fellows both through media and at an annual Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows dinner. ● Receive an annual Stipend of $1500.
Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow will: ● Attend at least one NCHC teaching workshop, organized by the URI Honors Program, prior to teaching first Honors course to share their teaching practices and learn about the latest in NCHC best practices. ● Teach at least one Honors or HPR course per year (or every other year, if department is constrained in terms of resources) ● Attend Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow meetings. ● Integrate the Honors Colloquium into their course offerings. ● Relay all Honors announcements in their courses.

Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows will be invited to: ● Present their proposed course in at least one “Launch your course” Distinguished Honors Teaching Studio. ● Serve as collaborator at one “Launch your course” Distinguished Honors Teaching Studio ● Present course taught at one “Recap/Revision Studio”; serve as evaluator/collaborator at one “Recap/Revision Studio” ● Become part of the governance and oversight structures of Honors program.
They may, for examples serve on the Honors curriculum committee or on its advisory committee. ● Contribute to the evaluation and review of their Distinguished Honors colleagues. ● Contribute to the Honors Program assessment. ● Contribute to promoting and raising the visibility of the Honors program and the URI Honors Institute. ● Mentor promising junior colleagues to become Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows Review and evaluation process ● A peer classroom observation during the first year of a. three-year term. ● After the first iteration of a course, a submission will be requested of a brief recap statement on how the course met the stated course objectives and the Honors program objective.

Suggestions will be invited on what could be improved, and what worked well, should be supported with examples of student work ● At the end of a three-year term, Distinguished Honors Faculty will be invited to deliver a presentation of one of their Honors courses at an Honors faculty showcase.

President's Update As we start this second meeting of the academic year, I want to give an update on the Faculty Senate budget situation. As many of you know, I have served on the Faculty Senate for over 20 years, including this being my third term as Senate President. In that time, under previous administrations, I have observed that the Senate operated on what I call a "tin-cup model" when it came to budget and resources. Senate leaders, especially committee chairs, are often faced with the difficult task of balancing Senate service with their regular faculty duties. Those who take on leadership roles rarely receive course relief or any other support that would make the extra commitment for Senate service worthwhile. Any time the Senate required resources, regardless of how small, we had to ask the provost for them. That model undermined the Senate's autonomy and our ability to exercise our academic freedom and engage in shared governance fully. But that was then and this is now. We are fortunate to have a dynamic and visionary President who can run faster and farther than any of us. Our Provost is a true Chief Academic Officer, a champion of faculty, and genuinely committed to academic excellence and shared governance. She cares deeply about empowering us to lead.

So, I am thrilled to report that Provost Wolfe wants to meet with Senate leadership to have a meaningful discussion about providing the Senate its own budget and empowering us to engage in our leadership roles. This represents an exciting opportunity for positive change that will benefit the Senate and the entire university community. I thank Provost Wolfe for her leadership on this. Please feel free to share any thoughts or suggestions as we embark on these important conversations about empowering our Faculty Senate. Thank you all for your time and dedication to shared governance.

1 Learning Outcomes and Oversight Committee (LOOC) Annual Report April 2010 As amended by the Faculty Senate on April 29, 2010 The charges to the committee (University Manual 5.84.10- 5.84.12): Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC) shall create policies for URI student learning outcomes assessment, data distribution and frequency of measurement at the university-wide level, with the approval of the Faculty Senate and the Provost.
Such policies would include but not be limited to external reporting and the release of assessment data, setting of standards for outcomes assessment, identification of strengths and limitations of existing assessment practices and recommendations for resource allocation to enhance assessment practices.
The committee shall provide advice and guidance to the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation relevant to faculty learning of best practices of student learning outcomes and assessment and oversee implementation and facilitation of approved policies by the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation.

The committee shall also develop an ongoing review of the learning outcomes assessment process, interpret external expectations for university-wide learning outcomes assessment, including those of accreditation bodies and facilitate internal communication across units regarding ways of meeting those expectations.
The members of the committee: As defined in the University Manual under section 5.84.13, the 27-member committee is representative of the entire University community.
LOOC includes 15 faculty members, representing all academic Colleges.
The listing of members of the 2009-2010 committee and their representation is on page 4 of this report.
Activities of 2009-2010: LOOC met monthly beginning November 2009, when a new chair was elected.

Priorities of the committee this academic were to: 1) Create a unified voice for student learning outcomes assessment at the University by: a) providing support and a reporting venue for the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (SLOAA) b) providing a common ground for programs working with graduate student learning outcomes assessment through cross-membership and monthly reports to LOOC by a member of the graduate council c) ensuring connectivity through cross-membership and monthly reports to LOOC by members of SAGE (Subcommittee for the Assessment of General Education) 2) Increase University awareness of the importance of student learning outcomes assessment by: a) ensuring appropriate LOOC representation on Academic Task Forces b) improving general faculty awareness through direct contact with LOOC representatives 3) Create policies for student learning outcomes assessment at the University, to be presented for formal vote by Faculty Senate on April 29, 2010 following review by the Provost (pages 2-3 of

2 this report).
These policies provide an important framework for University-directed student learning outcomes assessment of academic programs.
Establishment of Student Learning Outcomes Assessment Policies In fulfillment of a key element of its legislated mission, The University of Rhode Island Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC) recommends the following student learning outcomes assessment policies for approval by the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and Faculty Senate.
These policies represent both an institutional commitment to program-level assessment of student learning outcomes in order to advance our educational mission, and a response to external expectations from our accrediting body, New England Association of Schools and Colleges (NEASC), and the Rhode Island Board of Governors of Higher Education (RIBGHE).
The policies assure the important role of the faculty in guiding the process, setting the standards, drawing conclusions from the results, and promoting meaningful action in response to findings.
These policies directly promote learning as a central aspect of our mission.

Background In April 2004, the RIBGHE charged the three State institutions of higher education with engaging in institution-wide student learning outcomes assessment.
The 2005 NEASC Standards for Accreditation (4.44) requires the implementation of, “…a systematic and broad based approach to the assessment of student learning…” In 2006, URI established The Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (SLOAA) to support faculty in meeting RIBGHE’s student learning assessment reporting requirements.
The Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC) was established in the spring of 2007 as a joint committee of the Faculty Senate and Provost with representation from many important constituencies within the University.
Approval by the Faculty Senate and the President occurred at the April 19, 2007 Faculty Senate meeting, and approved University Manual language (09/06/2007) includes the following: 5.84.10 Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC) shall create policies for URI student learning outcomes assessment, data distribution and frequency of measurement at the university- wide level, with the approval of the Faculty Senate and the Provost.

Such policies would include but not be limited to external reporting and the release of assessment data, setting of standards for outcomes assessment, identification of strengths and limitations of existing assessment practices and recommendations for resource allocation to enhance assessment practices. #06- 07—25.
Proposal The central mission of LOOC is to facilitate the student learning outcomes assessment process to foster productive use of assessment at all levels.
This goal requires collaboration and full support from many parties, including the President, Provost, Deans, faculty, professional staff, and students.
The proposed policies provide clear guidance for the institution as we move forward in this essential process.

3 The University of Rhode Island Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC) recommends the following policies for approval by Provost DeHayes and the Faculty Senate: Policy#1.
Academic Program Engagement: All undergraduate, professional, and graduate academic programs, including General Education, shall be actively engaged in student learning outcomes assessment as evidenced by, but not limited to: a.
Published student learning outcomes that are clear statements of what students are expected to gain, achieve, demonstrate or know at the completion of the academic program.
These student learning outcomes shall be published on the program's website via a link to the website for the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation (SLOAA).
These student learning outcomes shall be periodically reviewed by the academic program for ongoing relevance. b.
A plan of student learning outcomes assessment that is endorsed by the program's faculty.

Plans should include a regular and predictable cycle for collecting and analyzing assessment data, for discussing curricular and programmatic changes, for implementing interventions, and for re-assessing the impact of implemented changes.
Outcomes assessment plans will be published on each program's website via a link to the SLOAA website. c.
Reports of student learning outcomes assessment that are provided to SLOAA using staggered cycles of no more than 3 years.
Cycles for accredited programs will be adjusted to decrease redundancy of effort.
Policy#2.
SLOAA Guidance for Academic Programs: Guidelines and schedules for preparation of outcomes assessment plans and reports shall be provided by SLOAA with the assistance and approval of the Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC).
SLOAA shall offer advice on the logistics of collecting assessment data, support for analyzing the results, and feedback on designing curricular and programmatic changes.
Rubrics for evaluating the plans and reports shall be generated by SLOAA and posted on its website.
Policy#3.

Evaluation of Plans and Reports: Student learning outcomes assessment plans and reports shall be submitted through SLOAA for evaluation and recommendations by LOOC.
Programs shall be notified directly of the results of the evaluation and whether modification is needed.
Summary reports shall be published on the SLOAA website.
LOOC shall provide a general summary of outcomes assessment in its annual report.
Policy#4.
University-Wide Student Learning Outcomes Assessment: With guidance from LOOC, SLOAA will work with the Office of Institutional Research and other university offices to collect, maintain, analyze, and distribute student learning outcomes assessment findings, derived from a variety of local and national sources.
SLOAA will identify patterns of student performance to inform ongoing program and institutional improvement.

The primary goal of the BS in Interdisciplinary Applied Artificial Intelligence is to prepare graduates who can apply artificial intelligence responsibly, creatively, and effectively across domains, integrating technical skills with ethical reasoning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and real-world problem solving.
The program emphasizes applied and lifelong learning, workforce relevance, and societal impact, ensuring that graduates are prepared for both immediate employment and long- term career adaptability.
It advances student success, retention, timely degree completion, and career readiness.
The program’s applied focus, interdisciplinary design, and integration of experiential learning opportunities support students in developing market- relevant skills that align with workforce needs.
By embedding internships, project-based learning, and applied AI coursework throughout the curriculum, the program enhances students’ engagement, persistence, and post-graduation outcomes while positioning URI graduates to succeed in a rapidly evolving, AI-enabled economy.

The vision is to provide students with deep knowledge of AI systems and expertise in transferring and applying AI to a variety of problem types.
This program will cover knowledge of the AI ecosystem including the ability to work in interdisciplinary teams with data and domain experts to collect, clean organize, and sample data, match the problem and data to the right intelligent computational tool (there are many types of AI, each with its strengths and weaknesses), tailor, build on top of, and adapt these tools to the problems at hand, support the safe, secure, ethical and accurate reporting of the results to domain experts, and guide teams in deciding if the analytical results make sense.
Students will learn how to use, tailor and augment AI so that the AI can serve as assistants in problem solving, with the human as the master, well versed in the interpretation, and ethical and societal implications of the use of the powerful AI that they will wield.
All of this is in the context of a world in which educators and potential employers are concerned with the lack of digital skills among today’s students and graduates.

To be well educated and prepared for the modern workplace, students must learn to acquire applied technology skills and also to transfer these technologies to specific problems as they arise.
Thus this program is not intended to train students to develop new AI, but to become experts in mastering, adapting, building upon, and deploying existing and evolving intelligent computational artifacts.
We will help students to master the AI tools of today but also help them to understand that these are only contemporary examples to sharpen their problem solving, and learning skills, and give them a leg up as they enter the workplace.
As the world changes and embraces new technologies such as digital twins, and quantum computing, both already inextricably intertwined with AI, we propose a major that is flexible enough that it can evolve with emerging intelligent technologies.
The program advances the University’s goals by preparing students to address complex real-world challenges through the responsible and creative application of emerging technologies.

The curriculum integrates applied coursework, project-based learning, and internships, ensuring that students develop both technical expertise and transferable skills that support career readiness and lifelong learning.
The program reflects the University’s commitment to interdisciplinary problem-solving and collaboration across colleges and departments.
The program also contributes to the University’s role in supporting economic development, innovation, and the future of work in Rhode Island and beyond.

Yes The BS in Interdisciplinary Applied Artificial Intelligence draws on a broad set of subject areas to support its interdisciplinary and applied focus, including: • Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning • Data Science, Statistics, and Analytics • Human– Computer Interaction and User Experience • Business Analytics and Decision Support Systems • Ethics of AI, Technology, and Society • Responsible and Explainable AI • Programming and Computational Thinking • Innovation, Entrepreneurship, and Design Thinking • Domain Applications of AI (e.g., business, finance, marketing, supply chain, environmental science, healthcare, social sciences) These subject areas align with existing strengths in the University Libraries’ collections across business, computer science, engineering, social sciences, and applied sciences.
The University Library currently provides access to many of the core resources needed to support this program, including journal articles, conference proceedings, and industry reports available through SpringerLink, Elsevier ScienceDirect, and ABI/Inform.
These resources are sufficient to support coursework, student research, and applied projects at launch.

Specialized datasets for applied AI projects Assignments across the curriculum are designed to progressively build students’ research, analytical, and communication skills.
Early coursework introduces students to finding and interpreting scholarly and professional sources related to AI and data-driven decision-making.
Upper-level courses emphasize interdisciplinary research, applied problem-solving, and project- based learning, requiring students to integrate library research with hands-on data analysis, modeling, and ethical evaluation.
Writing-intensive courses further support students’ ability to communicate AI-driven insights clearly to technical and non- technical audiences.
